name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Report: CT subsidizes bigger teacher pensions in wealthier school districts
description: Equable Institute found that retired teachers from CT's wealthiest districts get thousands more in pension payments from the state.
text:
There’s no shortage of discussion about inequity in Connecticut public education, but one aspect tends to fly under the radar: the teacher pension system.
The topic wasn’t addressed in the short list of policy ideas that came out of Gov. Ned Lamont’s Blue Ribbon Commission on K-12 Education Funding and Accountability. But researchers at Equable Institute, a bipartisan think tank specializing in public retirement systems, contend it is a key part of how wealthy districts outperform their less affluent peers.
In latest iteration of its “Who Benefits?” study — slated to publish soon — Equable found the districts with the biggest state pension subsidies have less teacher attrition on average than those with the smallest subsidies. And in general, it’s the wealthiest districts getting the biggest subsidies.
“We hear that … the funding formula for education is intended to equitably distribute resources. But then we see that wealthier towns are getting thousands of dollars more — in effect, to pay for teachers — than lower-resource towns,” said Anthony Randazzo, Equable executive director and the author of the report.
Here’s how that happens.
In Connecticut, each district negotiates its own teacher salaries. If a district has more property wealth — and thus more property tax revenue to work with — there’s a good chance it will be able to offer bigger salaries to its teachers. When teachers retire, their retirement benefits are based in large part on those salaries.
But while the district pays their salaries, it doesn’t pay their retirement benefits. The state does. This is where critics say the problem lies. 
There’s a general principle baked into Connecticut’s overall school funding system that results in more state money being allocated to less affluent districts. A town like Greenwich can raise more money with comparatively lower property taxes than, say, Hartford. In order to support equal educational opportunity, the state seeks to make up some portion of the difference.
The teacher retirement system does the opposite, Equable researchers say.
According to Equable, the state pays just under $27,000 per teacher in pension subsidies to the highest-poverty quartile of districts, which includes Bridgeport and Hartford. It pays over $32,000 per teacher to the lowest-poverty quartile, which includes New Canaan and Westport.
(The report bases poverty level on free and reduced price lunch eligibility, a commonly used proxy. The highest-poverty quartile has 61.6% of the state’s FRPL students. The lowest-poverty quartile has 5.6%.)
Equable argues that Connecticut’s teacher pension system exacerbates a problem that financially-strapped districts — often with higher-need populations — are already dealing with: teacher attrition. Its latest report found the state’s highest-poverty districts have an average teacher attrition rate of 11.74%. In the lowest-poverty districts, it’s 8.82%.
This is the first time the Equable study has looked at pension subsidies on a per-teacher basis. Randazzo said researchers sought to highlight the damage to educational fairness the often-overlooked system can cause: Districts with the greatest need are getting $5,000 less per teacher in pension subsidies than those with the lowest need.
By way of solutions, Equable has suggested districts with the largest teacher compensation packages pay a portion of the normal cost of pensions — that is, how much to pay into the system to cover all benefits earned in a given year. Connecticut is among the minority of states that do not currently require local districts to pay into a teacher retirement system.
If Equable’s proposal were adopted, the state would continue covering all pension costs for lower-wealth districts and could potentially reinvest its savings into the Education Cost Sharing grant.
Despite the lack of public discussion this year, the problems with the teacher retirement system aren’t unknown to the state’s education leaders. 
Govs. Dannel Malloy and Ned Lamont both took a swing at changing the system without success. The topic came up a handful of times this year in the Blue Ribbon Commission — whose stated task is to reimagine education funding from the ground up — but was not included in a list of policy ideas to advance as the group deliberates on its final recommendations.
“I think the solution is rooted more in state funding for both education and municipal aid so that districts have more resources to raise teacher salaries,” said Rep. Jennifer Leeper, D-Fairfield, who co-chairs the legislature’s Education Committee and sits on the Blue Ribbon Commission.
Cathryn Vaulman, Lamont’s director of communications, noted the governor’s unsuccessful attempt to change teacher pensions in the past.
“His efforts faced opposition in the Legislature, but he remains open to conversations about addressing inequities in the system,” Vaulman said.
Michael Morton of the School and State Finance Project said part of the problem is that pensions are not an easy topic to grasp. “It is fairly in the weeds. It is not the sexiest topic by any stretch of the imagination,” he said.
But Morton agreed with Equable’s overall findings. “That [pension] system has been in place for quite some time, and I think that inequity has only grown,” he said.
Morton said his organization has spent 11 years educating people on the ECS grant, an issue that has gained traction among the public and in the statehouse. That work hasn’t happened yet for teacher pensions.
That’s “one of the reasons why I think you need something to continue after the life of this [Blue Ribbon] commission, to regularly take up issues like this,” Morton said.
Unlike ECS, the proposed solution to pension inequity — that some towns kick in a portion of their own money — is a political hazard.
“The biggest challenge is, again, you’re asking wealthier communities to pay more. This is like the basic problem with any tax conversation,” Morton said.

title: New voter-backed trust fund could become South Dakota’s largest, state treasurer says
description: A trust fund endorsed by voters on Election Day could grow to become South Dakota’s largest, according to State Treasurer Josh Haeder. The state […]
text:
South Dakota State Treasurer Josh Haeder speaks with lawmakers at the Capitol in Pierre on Jan. 15, 2025. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)A trust fund endorsed by voters on Election Day could grow to become South Dakota’s largest, according to State Treasurer Josh Haeder.
Haeder made his comments during a recent meeting of the South Dakota Investment Council, which manages the state retirement system and trust funds that benefit schools, healthcare and the state budget. The state treasurer is a permanent member of the council, and last week’s meeting was Haeder’s last in the role. Republican Melissa Hull was elected to succeed fellow Republican Haeder, who is term-limited.
Voters endorsed Constitutional Amendment K to allow management of the state’s Unclaimed Property Trust Fund by the Investment Council, which will generate investment earnings to help fund state government.
Unclaimed property typically takes the form of unclaimed money from sources including bank accounts, stocks, life insurance payouts, uncashed checks and the contents of safe deposit boxes. If the entities holding the funds can’t find the owners within three years, the money can be transferred to the state. Anyone can claim their funds at any time, so the property is a perpetual liability for the state, but most unclaimed funds go uncollected.
Voters say yes to South Dakota Investment Council management of unclaimed property money

Haeder told the Investment Council on Nov. 17 that unclaimed property receipts for 2026 stood at $294 million. He’s proud, he said, to have pushed for a managed trust fund during his last year in office.
“That has the potential to become the largest trust fund in the state of South Dakota,” Haeder said.
The council manages four other trust funds: the Cement Plant Trust Fund, School and Public Lands Trust Fund, Education Enhancement Trust Fund, and Health Care Trust Fund. The largest by dollar amount is the Education Enhancement Trust Fund, seeded largely by money from a 1998 multi-state tobacco lawsuit settlement. That fund ended state fiscal year 2026 with a value of $842.5 million.
In a call with South Dakota Searchlight, Haeder said the reason the Unclaimed Property Trust Fund could grow to be the state’s largest is a matter of “simple math.”
More money comes in as unclaimed property every year, sometimes more than $200 million. Even after paying for marketing campaigns to convince people to collect their money and paying claims, the amount that would be transferred is likely to be significant.
In 2025, the state received $357 million in unclaimed property, according to the State Treasurer’s Annual Report, and paid out $49.6 million to claimants. That year was an unprecedented surge, but Haeder said annual receipts of $100 million or more are commonplace. That’s largely due to favorable laws and regulations that have attracted some national banks to place their headquarters in the state.
Within 10 years or so, Haeder said, the new trust fund could surpass $1 billion through annual allocations.
“It’s not a fund where we’re transferring a one-time dollar amount,” Haeder told Searchlight.
The idea behind creating the trust fund is that investing the money will do more for the state budget than gains from a small interest rate. 
The investment council will use some of the money to buy stocks and bonds and make other investments, pushing returns — and the resulting amount transferred to the state general fund — to a higher level.
The other four trust funds earned year-over-year returns between 8.2% and 9.3% in fiscal year 2026, according to the Investment Council’s latest annual report. 
Lawmakers passed a bill earlier this year sponsored by Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City, to put unclaimed property into a trust fund, but needed the recently approved state constitutional amendment to allow the Investment Council to put some of the money into stocks.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Specter of cuts to education draw ire, questions, calls for tax increases
description: A budget warning delivered to school systems across the state over the weekend, telling them to prepare budgets next year that are essentially flat from this year, is drawing the ire of some education advocates and questions from county leaders.
text:
Maryland schools systems were warned by state officials over the weekend to prepare budgets for next year that are essentially flat from this year, drawing the ire of some education advocates and questions from county leaders. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)A budget warning delivered to school systems across the state over the weekend is drawing the ire of some education advocates and questions from county leaders.
In a letter from Budget Secretary Yaakov “Jake” Weissmann this weekend, state school systems were asked to prepare budgets that are essentially flat compared to the current year. It comes as the state faces multibillion-dollar budget challenges, driven in part by historic education spending.
“We really do not know much about what this is going to mean for counties,” said Sarah Sample, associate policy director at the Maryland Association of Counties. “There’s still a lot of questions.”
State analysts project a nearly $3 billion budget shortfall in the coming year, the first of was is expected to be a shortfall up to $16 billion over five years.
Education spending is one of the drivers of that shortfall.
The letter sent to local school leaders contains no specifics about cuts or how counties will be affected. Instead, it appears to be more of a warning to locals to prepare for potential cuts by hewing the fiscal 2028 budget request as close to the current year as possible.
Budget secretary calls on school systems to prepare flat budgets for next year

In the current budget year, the state spent more than $10 billion on education.
Next year, the fund dedicated to paying for the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future, the state’s sweeping decade-long education reform plan, will be exhausted. Covering the costs will require Gov. Wes Moore (D) and state lawmakers to draw an estimated $1.8 billion from the general fund. Of that, only $500 million relates to new costs.
Senate Minority Leader Stephen S. Hershey (R-Upper Shore) said the letter “certainly appears to acknowledge that the looming shortfall is not simply a general revenue problem, but rather the state’s inability to sustain its existing Blueprint funding commitments.”
Cutting the Blueprint funding will not be easy. It passed after several years of hard-fought political battles and has vocal supporters.
Maryland State Education Association President Paul Lemle, in a statement, said cuts would “undermine progress” in student achievement, expanded technical career training, increased teacher pay, easing teacher shortages and adding support for high poverty schools.
“Its devastating consequences for our students are completely unacceptable,” Lemle said in his statement.
The teacher’s union estimates the cuts could result in a loss of $430 million in state aid. Another $270 million could come from county cuts, according to the union.
“This approach should be rejected,” said Lemle, who called for tax increases instead. “Our students deserve better. Make sure the ultra-wealthy and corporations are paying their fair share, rather than avoiding the contributions that the rest of us are making to fund the public schools and services we all depend on. Fund our schools—don’t set back their continued progress with these sweeping, across-the-board cuts.”
The letter was also criticized by the Public School Superintendent’s Association of Maryland.
“Maryland’s school systems have held up our end of the Blueprint bargain,” the association said in a statement. “The State must sustain its side of that partnership.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
The association called for increases for students with disabilities, and asked that one-year budget changes not result in ongoing reductions in per-pupil spending. And it asked for increased flexibility.
“Give local school systems meaningful flexibility to protect classroom instruction and direct staff and resources where students need them most,” the association said. “Districts will remain accountable for student outcomes and equitable access. State expectations for implementation should reflect what districts can realistically deliver with the funding provided.”
When the General Assembly returns in January, it will face some “very hard conversations” on the budget, Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) told business leaders last week.
Constitutionally, the only task the legislature must complete is passage of a balanced budget. Within that, the state is required to fund one priority — education.
Ferguson said it will taker all-options approach to solve the problem.
“The idea that we just solve it all with cuts, solve it all with just looking at keeping everything the same, is not realistic,” Ferguson said. “It is going to be a balanced approach. It is going to be a four-year plan. That means for the next 10 months, it is going to be very, very challenging.”
Pressure is mounting on state lawmakers from bond rating agencies, who want to see more fiscal discipline from the state. Instead of an annual effort to paper over long-term problems with fund balances and one-time fixes, the agencies expressed an interest in seeing an alignment of revenues and spending.
Analysts urge action on four years of projected gaps to get ahead of recession scenario

Moore, Ferguson  and House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel) have agreed, at least in principle, to craft a four-year budget solution, starting in January.
Other legislative leaders, meanwhile, warn that tax increases may be part of the solution.
“I’m expecting cuts and I’m expecting revenues,” said House Majority Leader Del. David Moon (D-Montgomery) during a Maryland Chamber of Commerce event last week.
The options range from increasing the sales tax or expanding it to include services — or both — as well as corporate tax changes and other proposals rejected in recent past sessions.
“They’re all the goodies and the oldies that have been floated in various things I’ve been reading,” Moon said. “I have no magic ball other than to say it seems like something has finally happened.”
Sample said many counties would likely see little to no relief if the state made changes to how it funds the Blueprint. She estimated maybe as many as six could potentially benefit.
A number of different scenarios each mean different outcomes for the counties. Some could result in additional costs shifted onto the counties, she cautioned.
In all, the state’s political subdivisions are paying $2.2 billion over anticipated costs for the education plan, according to the association.
“At most, this letter could signal an FY28 Blueprint cost reduction for, maybe, six or so of the poorest jurisdictions some of which have already raised taxes and fees to keep up with rising costs since implementation began, while absorbing millions in unrelated state cost shifts,” Sample said.
